summary: FireGuard is an interactive wildfire monitoring application that combines NASA FIRMS satellite observations from MODIS and VIIRS with weather data from Open-Meteo and location data from OpenStreetMap. Users can explore fire detections worldwide or search by place or coordinates over a selected date range. Nearby observations are grouped into events, which can be explored on a map. Selecting an event displays hourly temperature and wind conditions, observed hotspot displacement, and an approximate driving time from a nearby mapped fire station. By bringing information from multiple sources into one interface, FireGuard helps users review wildfire activity and supports greater awareness. Timely access to understandable information matters when assessing wildfire risks. FireGuard is for informational purposes: satellite detections are not necessarily confirmed fires, hotspot displacement is not a fire-spread forecast, and estimated driving time is not an emergency crew arrival time.
details:
FireGuard is a web-based wildfire monitoring and situational-awareness platform. It combines active-fire detections from NASA FIRMS, including MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations, and groups nearby observations into events using spatiotemporal clustering. Users can search by place name, coordinates, or the whole world, choose an observation date range, and explore detections on an interactive map. Selecting a fire reveals its observation details, hourly temperature and wind data from Open-Meteo, and an estimated hotspot displacement rate based on satellite observations. The app can also show an approximate driving route from a nearby mapped fire station and export event data as CSV. The interface supports English and Turkish.

The project aims to help users explore wildfire activity and access relevant environmental and location information in one place. Combining multiple data sources and presenting them on a map can make observations easier to review and support awareness and further investigation. FireGuard is an informational tool, not an official alert or dispatch system: satellite hotspots do not necessarily represent confirmed fires, estimated hotspot movement is not a fire-front forecast, and station driving times are not emergency-response ETAs.

The project was built primarily with Python. It uses Streamlit for the web interface, Folium and Streamlit-Folium for interactive mapping, Pandas and NumPy for data processing, and scikit-learn’s DBSCAN for clustering. NASA FIRMS provides satellite observations; Open-Meteo provides weather data; OpenStreetMap services—including Nominatim and Overpass—support place and station searches; and OSRM provides approximate road routes. GitHub Copilot was used as an AI coding assistant during development. No specialized hardware is required beyond a computer with internet access.

A key creative aspect of FireGuard is bringing satellite detections, local weather context, observed hotspot movement, and nearby mapped fire stations together in a single interactive workflow. The team considered data availability, geographic coverage, usability, performance, and the limitations of estimates derived from public data, and designed the interface to communicate those limitations clearly.
